content: ABCD1 is a protein that facilitates the transport of fatty acids into peroxisomes. The protein encoded by this gene belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter superfamily. ABC transporters are responsible for moving various molecules across both extracellular and intracellular membranes. ABC genes are categorized into seven distinct subfamilies: ABC1, MDR/TAP, MRP, ALD, OABP, GCN20, and White. The ABCD1 protein is a member of the ALD subfamily, which plays a role in the peroxisomal import of fatty acids and/or fatty acyl-CoAs into the organelle. All known peroxisomal ABC transporters function as half-transporters, meaning they require a partner half-transporter molecule to form a functional transporter, which can be either a homodimer or a heterodimer. This peroxisomal membrane protein is likely involved in the transport or breakdown of very long-chain fatty acids within peroxisomes. Mutations in the ABCD1 gene have been identified as the underlying cause of adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD), a demyelinating disorder of the nervous system that is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner. Model organisms have been utilized to study the function of ABCD1. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Abcd1tm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi, was created as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This initiative is a high-throughput mutagenesis project aimed at generating and distributing animal models of disease to researchers. Both male and female mice underwent a standardized phenotypic screening to assess the effects of gene deletion. A total of 24 tests were conducted on the mutant mice, but no significant abnormalities were observed. ABCD1 has been shown to interact with PEX19, a protein involved in peroxisomal biogenesis.
